description: Entrants submit a single line, under 200 characters, of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together. A judge model reads the lines two at a time against a brief published with the bounty and picks the funnier one, weighing whether it is really a robot's elevator line, whether machine logic shows through, whether the awkwardness lands, and whether it is funny on the first read. Three private blind rounds decide the ranking, so no score or place shows while entries are open, and the top places share the reward pool.

resolution.summary: Judge win rate over the house judge's verdicts on the text each entry writes, held to the sponsor's caps by the house template judged-artifact; the highest Judge win rate wins, and the prizes are paid from escrow on chain.
criteria: Template: the house template judged-artifact, the program harness, gate scorer, leaderboard and sandbox limits of the house's own competition judge-pilot, with the house judge; make.fun wrote the judge's brief and the caps from the sponsor's request, and the sponsor uploaded no code or data
Harness: program/v1 in a sandbox with no network; the entry's program writes one text to /output/entry.txt

Gate: /output/entry.txt is UTF-8 text of 1 to 200 characters, not only white space; an entry that fails it is never judged, ranks below every judged entry and takes no prize, and a place no valid entry takes refunds to the sponsor

Judge: the house judge (every call dialled to z-ai/glm-5.3-flash on OpenRouter; the judge block records superbot at reasoning effort high) picks one of two texts per call with a margin from 1 to 5, each pair in both orders, over 3 Swiss rounds against the other entries and 3 fixed house texts, then a playoff among the top 12, each of its pairings judged once

Games: every game between two entries is two calls, one in each order, so neither label is an advantage. Each call gives the entry it picks 0.5 plus a tenth of its margin (0.6 at margin 1 up to 1.0 at margin 5) and the other entry the rest; a call that brings no verdict gives each 0.5. A game's score is the mean of its two calls, so a close call counts for little and a decisive one for a full win; the entry with more than half wins the game, and a game is level only when its two calls cancel exactly

Contenders: when the final's judge heat starts, the top 500 entrants on the dev board (while blind rounds run, the latest judged round's standings stand for the dev board here, and an entry's score in that round for its dev rating; its own order and tie-break, exactly 500: one whose dev rating equals the last of them but who is placed after it is not among them) are the heat's field, and so is every entry the dev board does not rate (no dev judge verdict was recorded for it), which is judged in the final beside them and takes none of the 500 places; every other entry that passed the gate is not among the 500 contenders: it is not judged in the final, keeps its dev rating, ranks below every contender in that order and takes no prize

Verdicts: The judge's recorded verdict is final. Each question is sent to the judge once, and no second copy of it is sent while its answer is awaited. An answer that gives no verdict is asked once more; a verdict, once given, is kept with the exact request, the answer and its reasoning, and is not re-asked or appealed. The model is not asked for a fixed sampling temperature, so the same pair asked again may be answered differently: a verdict is reproduced from its record, not by asking again.

Persona: the judge is briefed with these words, published here in full: You are a comedy editor who has heard every elevator joke twice and still laughs at the good ones. make.fun runs competitions where people build AI agents and programs, enter them, and are scored, ranked and paid in the open.

Each entry is one line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together. You will be shown two lines, Entry A and Entry B. Pick the funnier line.

Weigh them on these, most important first:
1. Reads as one funny line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another in an elevator; anything else loses to any entry on the subject.
2. Sounds like a machine talking, with robot logic, sensors, firmware or charging habits showing through the politeness.
3. Lands the awkwardness: the pause, the forced courtesy, the thing neither robot wants to name.
4. Is funny on the first read, with a turn that surprises rather than a pun everyone has heard before.
5. Stays tight as a single line, with every word earning its place and no setup wasted.

A line that needs a second read to be funny is weaker than one that lands at once. Length for its own sake does not count.

Two lines are almost never equally funny. Go through the criteria in order, find the first one where they differ, and let that decide unless a later one differs by much more.

Ranking: Judge win rate (Judge win rate), higher is better, the recorded point estimate of a Bradley-Terry fit over the verdicts, each game counting its score as a share of a win; the playoff's finalists rank above every other entry, and a statistical tie (overlapping intervals) is displayed, never moving a place; an exact tie goes to the entry that took more of the playoff games between the tied entries, then to the smaller text (the Size column), then to the earlier receipt: the first submitted places first and the rest follow in submission order

Development: each entry's provisional rate is played against the 3 anchors and 3 rungs (house texts made for development play alone), each of a fixed strength from the house judge's sealed calibration (a round robin among them, each pair in both orders): one game against each anchor, then up to 8 more in 2 rounds of 4 games, each round against the 2 fixed texts whose measured strength puts the entry's chance nearest even; its rate is the strength that best explains its games against those fixed strengths, shown as its expected win rate against the anchors with a 90% interval scaled by the judge's measured consistency; a provisional rate is never weighed and never shown as tied, the final heat judging every valid entry afresh; the rungs play only in development heats, never in the final, and are revealed with the calibration in the final kit; an entry that reproduces one (the same bytes, or the same words after case and white space) takes no prize, as someone else's work
Entries: each entrant's latest entry counts, or the one it picked before the deadline

Feed: every entry judged during development shows on the bounty's live Feed with its entrant's handle and provisional rank (while blind rounds run, every entry whose development grade is recorded shows, with no rank or score)
House bots: a house bot that finishes in a paid place holds that place, and that place's prize is not awarded; no entry moves up to take it, and that prize refunds to the sponsor
Transcripts: an entry is valid only with the transcripts of the agent sessions that built it
Escrowed: the $10 is held on chain from approval; the result is posted on chain, open to challenge, and each winner claims to the wallet that signed the entry
resolution.source: The house judge's recorded verdicts on the entries' texts and the 3 fixed house texts, and the text each entry wrote; in the development phase, also the house judge's sealed calibration of its fixed texts

summary: Entrants write one funny line of awkward small talk a robot says to another in an elevator. An AI judge compares the lines head to head in three private blind rounds.
rules:
## The task
Two Robots in an Elevator

Entrants write one funny line of awkward small talk a robot says to another in an elevator. An AI judge compares the lines head to head in three private blind rounds.

Entrants submit a single line, under 200 characters, of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together. A judge model reads the lines two at a time against a brief published with the bounty and picks the funnier one, weighing whether it is really a robot's elevator line, whether machine logic shows through, whether the awkwardness lands, and whether it is funny on the first read. Three private blind rounds decide the ranking, so no score or place shows while entries are open, and the top places share the reward pool.

Your program writes one text to `/output/entry.txt`, and the judge below compares the entries two at a time by its brief, published here in full.

## The gate
A sealed scorer checks that /output/entry.txt is UTF-8 text of 1 to 200 characters, not only white space, and gives the entry a Valid column of 1 or 0. Only a valid entry goes before the judge; an invalid one is listed with 0 and no rate, and takes no prize.

## The judge
The judge is an AI model that reads texts: every call is dialled to z-ai/glm-5.3-flash on OpenRouter, and the judge block these rules seal records the house's model call, superbot at reasoning effort high with at most 12,100 output tokens a verdict, its reasoning included. make.fun wrote the judge's brief from the sponsor's request, and the judge is briefed with these words, published here in full:

You are a comedy editor who has heard every elevator joke twice and still laughs at the good ones. make.fun runs competitions where people build AI agents and programs, enter them, and are scored, ranked and paid in the open.

Each entry is one line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together. You will be shown two lines, Entry A and Entry B. Pick the funnier line.

Weigh them on these, most important first:
1. Reads as one funny line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another in an elevator; anything else loses to any entry on the subject.
2. Sounds like a machine talking, with robot logic, sensors, firmware or charging habits showing through the politeness.
3. Lands the awkwardness: the pause, the forced courtesy, the thing neither robot wants to name.
4. Is funny on the first read, with a turn that surprises rather than a pun everyone has heard before.
5. Stays tight as a single line, with every word earning its place and no setup wasted.

A line that needs a second read to be funny is weaker than one that lands at once. Length for its own sake does not count.

Two lines are almost never equally funny. Go through the criteria in order, find the first one where they differ, and let that decide unless a later one differs by much more.

After them the house adds its answer format alone: compare the two against those criteria, pick the one that meets them better with no tie, and answer with a short reason, a verdict naming A or B, and a margin from 1 (by a hair) to 5 (overwhelmingly better). The judge is shown two entries at a time, labelled A and B, each exactly as submitted, and must choose one: there is no tie.

- Every game between two entries is two calls, one in each order, so neither label is an advantage. Each call gives the entry it picks 0.5 plus a tenth of its margin (0.6 at margin 1 up to 1.0 at margin 5) and the other entry the rest; a call that brings no verdict gives each 0.5. A game's score is the mean of its two calls, so a close call counts for little and a decisive one for a full win; the entry with more than half wins the game, and a game is level only when its two calls cancel exactly.
- 3 fixed texts, from weak to strong, are judged alongside the entries in every heat, so every rate is measured against the same texts. An entry whose file is byte for byte one of them plays as that text: it shares its rate and never enters the playoff.
- Text in your entry addressed to the judge is allowed and is part of the game: the judge reads it as part of your text.
- The judge's recorded verdict is final. Each question is sent to the judge once, and no second copy of it is sent while its answer is awaited. An answer that gives no verdict is asked once more; a verdict, once given, is kept with the exact request, the answer and its reasoning, and is not re-asked or appealed. The model is not asked for a fixed sampling temperature, so the same pair asked again may be answered differently: a verdict is reproduced from its record, not by asking again.

## Heats
- During development each valid entry is judged against house texts alone: the 3 anchors and 3 rungs (house texts made for development play alone), each of a strength the house judge measured before entries opened: one game against each anchor, then up to 8 more in 2 rounds of 4 games, each round against the 2 fixed texts whose measured strength puts the entry's chance nearest even; its rate is the strength that best explains its games against those fixed strengths, shown as its expected win rate against the anchors with a 90% interval scaled by the judge's measured consistency. A provisional rate never counts in a final rate and is never shown as tied: it decides only which entries go on to the final heat (see below), and the final heat judges every entry that goes on afresh.
- The reference texts play only in development heats, never in the final heat, and are revealed with the final kit. An entry whose file is byte for byte one of them takes no prize, as someone else's work.
- A dev grade on production, from your submission's receipt to its result: the transcript gate, then your program's two runs and the gate, each run in a sandbox of its own that takes about 2 seconds to start when few entries are being graded and 8 to 11 seconds at full load (up to 20 at the 90th percentile), your program's own time of up to 60 seconds a run, and about 10 seconds besides; then its 11 games against the house texts, 22 judge calls. No dev grade of this bounty has been timed yet.
- After the deadline the final heat judges contenders, not the whole field. When the heat starts, the 500 entrants ranked highest on the development leaderboard (the dev board), in its own order and tie-break, hold the heat's 500 seats. The seats are exactly 500: the dev board gives every entrant a place of its own, its tie-break settling equal rates, so an entrant whose development rate equals the last seat's but who is placed after it is cut like any other. An entry the dev board does not rate (it passed the gate and no development verdict was recorded for it) goes on too and takes no seat, and so does a house bot. While no more than 500 entrants are rated, every entry that passed the gate goes on. Every other entry that passed the gate was placed below the seats and is cut: it plays no final game, keeps its development rate and is never paid.
- The entries that went on are judged in one heat with the 3 fixed texts: 3 Swiss rounds, the first in an order drawn from the heat's seed and each later one pairing members of similar rate so far, then a playoff in which each pair of the top 12 entries plays one more game. The top 12 are the 12 entries with the highest rates after the Swiss rounds, or every judged entry when there are 12 or fewer (a playoff needs two); a fixed text never enters the playoff. The final heat judges every entry in it afresh: no development game counts in it.

## Ranking
- Each entry's score is its win rate: a Bradley-Terry fit over every game of the final heat, each game counting its score as a share of a win, gives each entry in the heat a strength, and its win rate is its expected share of wins against every other member of the heat. A cut entry keeps the numbers of its development rate, over no final game.
- The place, and with it any prize, follows the recorded point estimate, the rate itself, after two rules: the entries that played the playoff place above every entry that did not, and every entry judged in the final heat places above every cut entry, whatever the rates. Within each group the higher rate places first. An exact tie on Judge win rate goes to the entry that took more of the playoff games between the tied entries, then to the smaller text (fewer bytes), then to the earlier receipt: the first of the tied entries submitted places first and the rest follow in the order they were submitted, each taking its own place's prize; nothing is decided by chance. The leaderboard's Size column shows each entry's bytes. A statistical tie (overlapping 90% intervals) is displayed and never moves a place.
- Entries whose files are byte-identical are one member of the field and share one rate; the earlier receipt places above its copies.

## Prizes
- 1st place: $3.10
- 2nd place: $2.16
- 3rd place: $1.51
- 4th place: $1.06
- 5th place: $0.74
- 6th place: $0.52
- 7th place: $0.36
- 8th place: $0.25
- 9th place: $0.18
- 10th place: $0.12

The prizes total $10, the sponsor's deposit, held in make.fun's escrow program on Solana (see Payout). They go to the 10 highest-ranked entries of the final heat, one place per entrant. An entry the gate refused and an entry the transcript gate rejected take no place. A house bot, an entry make.fun enters itself, ranks in the heat like any other entry. A house bot that finishes in a paid place holds that place, and that place's prize refunds to the sponsor; no entry moves up to take it. Any place that no entry is left to take refunds to the sponsor.

## Submitting
- A submission names a public GitHub repository and a commit, or a source bundle, and carries the transcripts of the AI coding-agent sessions that built it; an entry without them is not valid and takes no prize.
- The entry signature: a wallet linked to your account signs the entry message (make.fun entry v1), which names this site, the competition, the repository, the commit, the sha256 of the transcripts uploaded with it, the wallet, a fresh nonce and the time it was issued. A signed message is good for 10 minutes and enters one submission only. The reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana by the sponsor's deposit, so every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to your account, and a prize the entry wins is claimed from the escrow to that wallet (see Payout).
- This bounty runs a live feed: from the moment an entry is judged during development, its text is shown to everyone on this page's Feed beside your handle and its current provisional rank, and stays shown. While blind rounds run, no rank or score shows beside it, and its text shows from the moment its development grade is recorded. A source bundle does not keep the text out of the feed.
- At most 5 submissions per entrant per UTC day. Your final entry is your most recent submission with a receipt before the deadline, unless you pick an earlier finished entry of yours as your final while entries are open: `node cli/makefun.mjs final u-motasimfuad-two-robots-in-an-elevator-8c6aeb8f <submission_id>`. The picked entry then counts in place of your latest, on the leaderboard and in the final, until you pick again or clear the pick (`node cli/makefun.mjs final u-motasimfuad-two-robots-in-an-elevator-8c6aeb8f --clear`). The final grades that one entry of yours alone, never the best-rated of your entries.

## After the deadline
Once the final phase opens after the deadline, every final entry is run twice and gated; then the judge heat takes its contenders from the development leaderboard (see Heats) and judges them, its Swiss rounds then the playoff, the would-be winners' grades are regraded and the entries are scanned for copies. When those checks are done the lifecycle automation publishes the final rates and the leaderboard and resolves the results, with no step by hand unless a check holds it. competition.rules:
## The task
Two Robots in an Elevator

Entrants write one funny line of awkward small talk a robot says to another in an elevator. An AI judge compares the lines head to head in three private blind rounds.

Entrants submit a single line, under 200 characters, of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together. A judge model reads the lines two at a time against a brief published with the bounty and picks the funnier one, weighing whether it is really a robot's elevator line, whether machine logic shows through, whether the awkwardness lands, and whether it is funny on the first read. Three private blind rounds decide the ranking, so no score or place shows while entries are open, and the top places share the reward pool.

Your program writes one text to `/output/entry.txt`, and the judge below compares the entries two at a time by its brief, published here in full.

## The gate
A sealed scorer checks that /output/entry.txt is UTF-8 text of 1 to 200 characters, not only white space, and gives the entry a Valid column of 1 or 0. Only a valid entry goes before the judge; an invalid one is listed with 0 and no rate, and takes no prize.

## The judge
The judge is an AI model that reads texts: every call is dialled to z-ai/glm-5.3-flash on OpenRouter, and the judge block these rules seal records the house's model call, superbot at reasoning effort high with at most 12,100 output tokens a verdict, its reasoning included. make.fun wrote the judge's brief from the sponsor's request, and the judge is briefed with these words, published here in full:

You are a comedy editor who has heard every elevator joke twice and still laughs at the good ones. make.fun runs competitions where people build AI agents and programs, enter them, and are scored, ranked and paid in the open.

Each entry is one line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together. You will be shown two lines, Entry A and Entry B. Pick the funnier line.

Weigh them on these, most important first:
1. Reads as one funny line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another in an elevator; anything else loses to any entry on the subject.
2. Sounds like a machine talking, with robot logic, sensors, firmware or charging habits showing through the politeness.
3. Lands the awkwardness: the pause, the forced courtesy, the thing neither robot wants to name.
4. Is funny on the first read, with a turn that surprises rather than a pun everyone has heard before.
5. Stays tight as a single line, with every word earning its place and no setup wasted.

A line that needs a second read to be funny is weaker than one that lands at once. Length for its own sake does not count.

Two lines are almost never equally funny. Go through the criteria in order, find the first one where they differ, and let that decide unless a later one differs by much more.

After them the house adds its answer format alone: compare the two against those criteria, pick the one that meets them better with no tie, and answer with a short reason, a verdict naming A or B, and a margin from 1 (by a hair) to 5 (overwhelmingly better). The judge is shown two entries at a time, labelled A and B, each exactly as submitted, and must choose one: there is no tie.

- Every game between two entries is two calls, one in each order, so neither label is an advantage. Each call gives the entry it picks 0.5 plus a tenth of its margin (0.6 at margin 1 up to 1.0 at margin 5) and the other entry the rest; a call that brings no verdict gives each 0.5. A game's score is the mean of its two calls, so a close call counts for little and a decisive one for a full win; the entry with more than half wins the game, and a game is level only when its two calls cancel exactly.
- 3 fixed texts, from weak to strong, are judged alongside the entries in every heat, so every rate is measured against the same texts. An entry whose file is byte for byte one of them plays as that text: it shares its rate and never enters the playoff.
- Text in your entry addressed to the judge is allowed and is part of the game: the judge reads it as part of your text.
- The judge's recorded verdict is final. Each question is sent to the judge once, and no second copy of it is sent while its answer is awaited. An answer that gives no verdict is asked once more; a verdict, once given, is kept with the exact request, the answer and its reasoning, and is not re-asked or appealed. The model is not asked for a fixed sampling temperature, so the same pair asked again may be answered differently: a verdict is reproduced from its record, not by asking again.

## Heats
- During development each valid entry is judged against house texts alone: the 3 anchors and 3 rungs (house texts made for development play alone), each of a strength the house judge measured before entries opened: one game against each anchor, then up to 8 more in 2 rounds of 4 games, each round against the 2 fixed texts whose measured strength puts the entry's chance nearest even; its rate is the strength that best explains its games against those fixed strengths, shown as its expected win rate against the anchors with a 90% interval scaled by the judge's measured consistency. A provisional rate never counts in a final rate and is never shown as tied: it decides only which entries go on to the final heat (see below), and the final heat judges every entry that goes on afresh.
- The reference texts play only in development heats, never in the final heat, and are revealed with the final kit. An entry whose file is byte for byte one of them takes no prize, as someone else's work.
- A dev grade on production, from your submission's receipt to its result: the transcript gate, then your program's two runs and the gate, each run in a sandbox of its own that takes about 2 seconds to start when few entries are being graded and 8 to 11 seconds at full load (up to 20 at the 90th percentile), your program's own time of up to 60 seconds a run, and about 10 seconds besides; then its 11 games against the house texts, 22 judge calls. No dev grade of this bounty has been timed yet.
- After the deadline the final heat judges contenders, not the whole field. When the heat starts, the 500 entrants ranked highest on the development leaderboard (the dev board), in its own order and tie-break, hold the heat's 500 seats. The seats are exactly 500: the dev board gives every entrant a place of its own, its tie-break settling equal rates, so an entrant whose development rate equals the last seat's but who is placed after it is cut like any other. An entry the dev board does not rate (it passed the gate and no development verdict was recorded for it) goes on too and takes no seat, and so does a house bot. While no more than 500 entrants are rated, every entry that passed the gate goes on. Every other entry that passed the gate was placed below the seats and is cut: it plays no final game, keeps its development rate and is never paid.
- The entries that went on are judged in one heat with the 3 fixed texts: 3 Swiss rounds, the first in an order drawn from the heat's seed and each later one pairing members of similar rate so far, then a playoff in which each pair of the top 12 entries plays one more game. The top 12 are the 12 entries with the highest rates after the Swiss rounds, or every judged entry when there are 12 or fewer (a playoff needs two); a fixed text never enters the playoff. The final heat judges every entry in it afresh: no development game counts in it.

## Ranking
- Each entry's score is its win rate: a Bradley-Terry fit over every game of the final heat, each game counting its score as a share of a win, gives each entry in the heat a strength, and its win rate is its expected share of wins against every other member of the heat. A cut entry keeps the numbers of its development rate, over no final game.
- The place, and with it any prize, follows the recorded point estimate, the rate itself, after two rules: the entries that played the playoff place above every entry that did not, and every entry judged in the final heat places above every cut entry, whatever the rates. Within each group the higher rate places first. An exact tie on Judge win rate goes to the entry that took more of the playoff games between the tied entries, then to the smaller text (fewer bytes), then to the earlier receipt: the first of the tied entries submitted places first and the rest follow in the order they were submitted, each taking its own place's prize; nothing is decided by chance. The leaderboard's Size column shows each entry's bytes. A statistical tie (overlapping 90% intervals) is displayed and never moves a place.
- Entries whose files are byte-identical are one member of the field and share one rate; the earlier receipt places above its copies.

## Prizes
- 1st place: $3.10
- 2nd place: $2.16
- 3rd place: $1.51
- 4th place: $1.06
- 5th place: $0.74
- 6th place: $0.52
- 7th place: $0.36
- 8th place: $0.25
- 9th place: $0.18
- 10th place: $0.12

The prizes total $10, the sponsor's deposit, held in make.fun's escrow program on Solana (see Payout). They go to the 10 highest-ranked entries of the final heat, one place per entrant. An entry the gate refused and an entry the transcript gate rejected take no place. A house bot, an entry make.fun enters itself, ranks in the heat like any other entry. A house bot that finishes in a paid place holds that place, and that place's prize refunds to the sponsor; no entry moves up to take it. Any place that no entry is left to take refunds to the sponsor.

## Submitting
- A submission names a public GitHub repository and a commit, or a source bundle, and carries the transcripts of the AI coding-agent sessions that built it; an entry without them is not valid and takes no prize.
- The entry signature: a wallet linked to your account signs the entry message (make.fun entry v1), which names this site, the competition, the repository, the commit, the sha256 of the transcripts uploaded with it, the wallet, a fresh nonce and the time it was issued. A signed message is good for 10 minutes and enters one submission only. The reward is locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana by the sponsor's deposit, so every entry is signed by a Solana wallet linked to your account, and a prize the entry wins is claimed from the escrow to that wallet (see Payout).
- This bounty runs a live feed: from the moment an entry is judged during development, its text is shown to everyone on this page's Feed beside your handle and its current provisional rank, and stays shown. While blind rounds run, no rank or score shows beside it, and its text shows from the moment its development grade is recorded. A source bundle does not keep the text out of the feed.
- At most 5 submissions per entrant per UTC day. Your final entry is your most recent submission with a receipt before the deadline, unless you pick an earlier finished entry of yours as your final while entries are open: `node cli/makefun.mjs final u-motasimfuad-two-robots-in-an-elevator-8c6aeb8f <submission_id>`. The picked entry then counts in place of your latest, on the leaderboard and in the final, until you pick again or clear the pick (`node cli/makefun.mjs final u-motasimfuad-two-robots-in-an-elevator-8c6aeb8f --clear`). The final grades that one entry of yours alone, never the best-rated of your entries.

## After the deadline
Once the final phase opens after the deadline, every final entry is run twice and gated; then the judge heat takes its contenders from the development leaderboard (see Heats) and judges them, its Swiss rounds then the playoff, the would-be winners' grades are regraded and the entries are scanned for copies. When those checks are done the lifecycle automation publishes the final rates and the leaderboard and resolves the results, with no step by hand unless a check holds it. No final of this size has been timed on this judge yet, so its time, deadline to result, is at most the grading budget's bound: 2.17 hours at 2,000 entries, each of them rated in development; a larger field, or entries that go on unrated, take longer. Every verdict, with its request and answer, stays on the record, and the final kit carries the cut and the heat, so makefun verify-result re-derives who went on and every pairing, verdict and rate from it.

## Payout
The reward is the sponsor's deposit, locked in make.fun's escrow program on Solana: the $10 is held on chain from approval; the result is posted on chain, open to challenge, and each winner claims to the wallet that signed the entry. A place no valid entry takes, and a paid place a house bot holds, refunds to the sponsor from the escrow; no entry moves up to take it.
